item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
My problem there is that the article specifically references that the sky was blue before the whole shift thing. Am I to suppose that the modern interpretation of blue had existed as a color prior to the shift, and that the sky was previously another color (a gray-that-used-to-be-blue, as Tuned put it before), or is it the case that the SCP created a new color that was to be blue? If either is the case, wouldn't a direct swapping of the old blue for the new blue take place, regardless of whether we are referring to the sky or just film/ink/pixel picture of it?

I think my main issue is that the article treats pictures as immune to the effect of the SCP when I can't find a logical way that they would be. At the end of the day, they are physical things made of atoms that reflect light. If the sky can be changed, then the precedent is set that inorganic things can be changed, and that would logically extend to include and influence the colors of ink, film, pixels, LEDs, and anything else that could be used to display a picture.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I could be understanding this wrong, however. Perhaps the modern "blue" did exist as a color or concept before the infection, but it was not called blue?

In real life, the color blue doesn't exist in most languages until fairly recently (and there are extant languages where it still doesn't). This is why Homer's Aegean is "wine-dark". People generally only need a color word when that color is a dye or pigment that you can make.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I know Tuned has tried to explain the picture thing to other users, but I'm having a hard time making all of it seem logically consistent.

+ Open
- Close

If I am to get the skip correctly, our modern understanding of color was akin to an infection, spreading from one thing to another via direct exposure, until everything was in our current colors. I also assume that this "infection" extends to ALL things, not just organic material.

Therein lies my issue with this whole thing. I don't know if this infection is retrocausal or not. Ink, being a physical thing that reflects light just like anything else, must be susceptible to "infection". Given that things before the infection were always a specific color, that corresponding color of ink would be used to depict it. For example, the sky was "blue" before infection, and then was transmuted to the modern blue once infected. Similarly, a picture of the sky was "blue" before infection, but the ink used to print said photo is susceptible to infection, and since it was an accurate recreation of the color of the sky, logically it should react to the infection in the same manner as the sky did, meaning that an old "pre-infection" picture of the sky should be altered by exposure to the color infection to look how we currently see blue. Obviously, so many years after every conceivable thing has been exposed to the new system of color, there would not be any ink left that has not been exposed, and so no "black and white" images should exist.

This article treats the color of the subject and its picture to be two separate things, but if the modern interpretation of "blue" did not exist before this phenomenon, then ink that was extant before this time could not both reproduce this new color and the original color at the same time. Instead, it has to be a straight palate swap. All blue ink has to have directly changed from the old interpretation to the new upon exposure.

I get how this might work for actual film photographs, but even then, film simply reflects the same wavelengths as what it was exposed to. That means if something was blue before, then a film picture would reflect the same wavelength that the actual object does. Hence, when the reflected wavelengths of the object are changed to match modern blue, then logically the reflected wavelengths of the photograph would be changed by the infection to match once it has been summarily exposed.

I understand the example of taking a picture and then dying ones hair and obviously not expecting the photo to change, but if this color infection of sorts affected everything that has a color, then film and ink would have to be included as susceptible to said effects. If my hair was changed by this anomaly in one way, then naturally anything that previously reflected the exact same wavelengths as my hair would also be affected in the same way, including pictures and film of my hair.


I could be understanding this wrong, however. Perhaps the modern "blue" did exist as a color or concept before the infection, but it was not called blue?

item.title: Wonderfully Done
item.content:encoded: Remarkably easy +1 from me. Probably the single best example of an EX category SCP. Well written, interesting in concept, and thought-provoking! While i understand why some people had a hard time understanding what this was going for, i believe those with the mindset to fundamentally understand this one agree that it stands well above the competition in EX class and deserves its high spot on the total rating listings.

"My hands are of your color, but I shame to wear a heart so white.”

"My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damasked, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;"

"Will all the water in the ocean wash this blood from my hands? No, instead my hands will stain the seas scarlet, turning the green waters red."

I think why I don't like this SCP is because the illusion is too grand, the consequences too far reaching. It would be a bit like claiming that Australia doesnt exist and has never existed, and so the Foundation intercepts and fakes all letters, communications, mind wipes all Australian tourists, etc. It's a monumental task and it doesn't fit in with my headcanon of the Foundation at all. I like to think that the Foundation is in our real life Earth, cleverly blending in but still there if you look hard enough, with plenty of mystery uncontained. This points to a Foundation who could basically convince the Earth that aliens didn't invade and destroy all of Africa, even if they did.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: This SCP isn't about hard-science physical explanations for anomalies, though, so while your opinion is valid I don't think you're being fair to the article. It's about showing us how something as immutable and inherent as color become changable; transforming what we take absolutely for granted into evidence of an event and cover-up on a huge scale, and spreading that cover-up beyond the article to include the reader themselves. We are sight-oriented creatures, and this article offers a new perspective on everything we've ever seen by turning both color and black-and-white images into artifacts of an enormous change.

There are plenty of funny non-J's that I have upvoted. Don't get me wrong, I am firmly NOT in the camp that the Foundation needs to be grimdark all the time. For instance, I upvoted Skip, the Toaster that is Me, even the Paper Towel Fusion Battery, and the spoon that bends you.

I will say that I read the Calvin and Hobbes comic before I saw this SCP.

I don't like this one because its just too silly/stupid to be taken seriously. So "certain photography techniques" started giving the universe color? So what about all of the beautiful descriptions of different colors for the past 10,000 years? What about paintings that and drawings that magically colored in correctly to what they were depicting? What about light from stars that hasn't reached us yet? What about… I dunno… PHYSICS?

Its funny, in the Calvin and Hobbes sense, but there's so many blatant issues with this phenomenon that it just doesn't work. I can't upvote this except as a joke, which it apparently wasn't intended to be. And if it was, then it should be a -J.

item.content:encoded: I keep seeing this criticism on various SCPs that aren't completely serious about their subject matter, and now I'm seeing it on one that treats its subject matter seriously. It's rather baffling. An SCP doesn't have to be horrifying, grimdark and serious. For an SCP-J, you have to look at it and go "Wait, really?" "No, not really." For a regular skip, you go "Wait, really?" "Yes, Really." This one firmly falls into the second category. I fail to see any even remotely humorous elements in this.
